consoleText:
ARISTOTELIAN SYLLOGISM TESTING PROGRAM
Aristotelian syllogisms consist of two premises followed by a
conclusion. The first (Major) premise connects the predicates M
and P, the second (Minor) premise connects the predicates S and
M, while the Conclusion connects the predicates S and P. Four
different types of logical connection are available, with a
traditional shorthand code using the vowels A, E, I and O:
    A     All Fs are G.       E     No F is G.
    I     Some F is G.        O     Some F is not G.
There are thus 4 possible relations in the Major Premise, 4 in
the Minor Premise, and 4 in the Conclusion (so 64 combinations
overall), but in addition, there are four different "Figures",
which indicate the order of the predicates in each proposition:
   Figure 1   Major: M-P   Minor: S-M   Conclusion: S-P
   Figure 2   Major: P-M   Minor: S-M   Conclusion: S-P
   Figure 3   Major: M-P   Minor: M-S   Conclusion: S-P
   Figure 4   Major: P-M   Minor: M-S   Conclusion: S-P
Hence there are 256 possible syllogisms altogether. Here is the
syllogism of Figure 1 coded "EIO":
   No M is P;  Some S is M;  therefore  Some S is not P.
And here is the syllogism of Figure 4 coded "AEO":
   All Ps are M;  No M is S;  therefore  Some S is not P.
The vowel codes were used in the Middle Ages as mnemonics for
the forms of syllogism that were accepted as valid - in these
cases "Ferio" (1:EIO) and "Calemos" (4:AEO) respectively. But
note that Calemos is invalid (i.e. its premises can be true and
yet its conclusion turn out false) if we allow a world in which
there is no S at all. Aristotle's theory takes for granted that
all three predicates are at least satisfied by something.

Now press "f" or "F" for Fregean validity testing, which does not
assume that the relevant predicates M, P and S are satisfied
by anything; press "a" or "A" for Aristotelian validity testing.
Capital "F" or "A" will display all 256 possible population types
as they are generated and tested.
